title: In Defense of Being Wrong
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post examines defensive attribution, the common tendency to credit successes to our own skill while blaming failures on luck, circumstances or other people. After a mistake, people reflect in order to learn, but their self-protective instincts bend the analysis and understate their own role. The same bias colors how people judge decisions and forecasts, claiming insight when they turn out right and finding outside causes when they do not. The author treats this as universal but says good leaders guard against making it a habit. Their remedy is to focus on solutions and consequences rather than hunting for blame, since failure is compounded when attribution is its only ally.
points: Defensive attribution protects self-esteem by assigning bad outcomes to external factors and good ones to personal ability.
The bias undermines learning from failure because the honest review of one's own part gets skipped.
It also affects decisions and forecasts, which are credited to skill when right and explained away when wrong.
The leadership response is to prioritize a remedy over assigning blame.
quotes: People don’t like to be wrong. They like to fail even less. This is especially true with big mistakes and faulty predictions.
But a funny thing happens on the way to drawing a conclusion. People commonly underestimate their own role and actions in creating the outcome.
Instead, they look for answers that don’t include them. They have a need to attribute negative outcomes to anyone but the person staring back in the mirror.

Defensive attribution serves to protect the self-esteem of those on the losing side of outcomes. The vulnerability of admitting they were wrong or failed is just too much to bear sometimes. That’s why everyone attributes outcomes defensively on occasion.
To learn and improve, it is only natural to seek the reasons why outcomes occurred. But our defensiveness can get in the way of accuracy.

Given the tendency to attribute success to ourselves and failures to others, good leaders challenge themselves to rise above self-protection and deal with the consequences instead. They seek a remedy rather than blame. That’s because they know that failure is compounded when attribution is its only ally.
